chapter.title: Fish and Crustaceans, Molluscs and Other Aquatic Invertebrates

page.h1: HTS Chapter 03: Fish and Crustaceans, Molluscs and Other Aquatic Invertebrates — U.S. Export Rules & Ways to Pay Less Abroad

seo.title: U.S. Seafood Export Rules: NOAA Certificates, Schedule B & More
seo.shortDescription: What the U.S. requires before you export lobster, salmon, pollock and other seafood: NOAA export health certificates, FDA export lists, Schedule B, USFWS and CITES rules, AES.

intro: Most U.S. seafood leaves the country without an export licence: fish, lobster and other shellfish are EAR99, so the federal steps are the usual ones — find the Schedule B number, screen the buyer and file the export in AES. What takes work is the buyer's food-safety paperwork, and in the U.S. that runs through two agencies. **NOAA's Seafood Inspection Program** is the U.S. authority that signs seafood **export health certificates**, and they must be issued before the product ships; China, the EU, Viet Nam, Taiwan, Brazil and Australia require one, and many accept product only from NOAA-approved plants. **FDA** keeps the export lists of U.S. seafood plants that China, the EU, the UK and Saudi Arabia require. Live fish shipped for anything other than food, such as glass eels for fish farms, and species listed under CITES (sharks, for example) also need U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service paperwork.

steps.title: Find the Schedule B number
steps.whatToDo: Look up the 10-digit Schedule B number for each product with the Census Bureau's free search tool. Its first six digits are the same as the HS code every country uses, so it also tells you which line of the buyer's tariff applies. The U.S. import (HTS) number and the Schedule B number match only to six digits.
steps.when: Every export. It goes on the export filing (the last step) and on the commercial invoice.
steps.chapterNote: Live lobster is 0306.32 and frozen lobster 0306.12; frozen fish roe is 0303.91, frozen sockeye 0303.11 and other frozen Pacific salmon (pink, chum, coho, king) 0303.12; Alaska pollock is 0303.67 whole, 0304.75 as frozen fillets and 0304.94 as frozen meat or surimi; frozen squid is 0307.43 and live geoduck and other clams 0307.71. The first six digits are the HS code on the Overview.

steps.title: Screen the buyer and everyone in the deal
steps.whatToDo: Check the buyer, the end user and any agent against the Consolidated Screening List. It combines the Commerce lists (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified, Military End-User), the State Department lists and the Treasury (OFAC) sanctions lists of parties you may not deal with, or may deal with only under a licence.
steps.when: Every export, before you accept the order.
steps.chapterNote: Seafood often moves through traders and reprocessors in Hong Kong, China, Thailand and Viet Nam. Screen the consignee and, where you know it, the final buyer.

steps.title: Check whether you need an export licence
steps.whatToDo: Find the product's Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) on the Commerce Control List. Most goods are not listed and are EAR99. For a listed ECCN, look up the destination on the Commerce Country Chart under each reason for control: an X means a licence is needed unless a licence exception applies. Even EAR99 goods need a licence for embargoed countries and for restricted end users or end uses.
steps.when: Every export of goods subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
steps.chapterNote: Fish, crustaceans and molluscs are EAR99, so no Commerce licence is needed unless the destination or end user is restricted (see the sanctions step). Wildlife permits for live fish and CITES-listed species are separate; see the agency rules below.

steps.title: Check sanctions on the destination
steps.whatToDo: Check the destination against OFAC's sanctions programs and the EAR's embargo rules. Cuba, Iran and North Korea have country-wide rules, and Syria still needs a Commerce licence for most items; Russia and Belarus need a licence for any item with an ECCN. Several programs have special permissions for food and medicine.
steps.when: Exports to a sanctioned or embargoed country, or to a listed person anywhere.
steps.chapterNote: NOAA states it cannot issue export certificates for seafood bound for Russia, so buyers there cannot clear U.S. seafood. Food sales to Cuba and Iran run under special OFAC and BIS rules; check the current program before quoting any sanctioned destination.

steps.title: File the export in AES (Electronic Export Information)
steps.whatToDo: You (the U.S. principal party in interest) or your freight forwarder file the EEI in the Automated Export System — free through ACE AESDirect — and put the confirmation number (ITN) on the shipping documents. File at least 24 hours before an ocean shipment is loaded, 2 hours before a flight departs, or 1 hour before a truck reaches the border. Not filing can cost a civil penalty of up to $17,412 per violation.
steps.when: When one Schedule B number in one shipment to one buyer is worth over $2,500, and at any value when the shipment needs a Commerce licence or a DEA permit or declaration, or ships an EAR item to Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Syria, or a Commerce Control List item to China, Russia or Venezuela.
steps.chapterNote: A box of live lobster or a container of frozen fish is almost always worth more than $2,500 per Schedule B number, so plan to file in AES.

rules.agency: NOAA Fisheries, Seafood Inspection Program (U.S. Department of Commerce)
rules.title: Export health certificate: NOAA is the U.S. competent authority that signs seafood export health certificates, and a certificate must be requested and issued before the product ships. China, the EU, Viet Nam, Taiwan (since August 12, 2025), Brazil and Australia require one with every shipment; South Korea requires one for live fish and shellfish and for unprocessed fresh or frozen abalone, oysters and shrimp; Japan only for live raw oysters, and Thailand and Hong Kong set no requirement. Many buyers (China, Viet Nam, Brazil, Australia) also accept product only from plants that are NOAA “Approved Establishments”. NOAA's export pages list each country's certificate and conditions.

FDA export lists: China, the EU, the UK and Saudi Arabia accept seafood only from plants on a list the competent authority sends them, and FDA keeps those lists. A plant applies through FDA's Export Listing Module (ELM); the EU publishes updates about 10 weeks after FDA sends them and accepts certificates only for listed plants. China also asks for current third-party certification of compliance with Chinese standards, uploaded in ELM. For EU certificates signed on or after September 3, 2026, aquaculture products need a declaration on antimicrobial use.

EU catch documentation: wild-caught seafood for the EU needs proof of legal harvest under the EU's illegal-fishing rules. NOAA's online system issues a Legal Harvest document for fish caught by U.S.-flagged vessels together with the EU health certificate; foreign-caught fish processed in the U.S. needs an “Annex IV” catch certificate instead. NOAA also asks for a Legal Harvest certificate for cooked crab sold to Japan.

citations.label: NOAA: EU export health certificates and Legal Harvest documents

rules.agency: NOAA Seafood Inspection Program and FDA, with the General Administration of Customs of China (GACC)
rules.title: China: every processor must be a NOAA Approved Establishment and on FDA's China export list, from which the U.S. side recommends plants to China's customs agency (GACC) for registration, and each shipment needs NOAA's bilingual China health certificate (a separate version covers live products). The Chinese importer must also be registered with GACC. GACC Decree No. 280, in force since June 1, 2026, replaced Decree No. 248: aquatic products stay in the group registered on the exporting country's recommendation, registration runs five years and renews automatically. USDA's Beijing office advises U.S. seafood exporters to keep following FDA's procedures rather than apply to GACC directly.

citations.label: NOAA: export requirements by country (A–F), China

rules.agency: Ministry of Food and Drug Safety of Korea (MFDS), with NOAA
rules.title: South Korea: overseas plants must be pre-registered with MFDS, by the importer or the exporter, at least 7 days before the import declaration. NOAA's health certificate is needed for live fish, live shellfish and crustaceans and unprocessed fresh or frozen abalone, oysters and shrimp, and a catch certificate where Korea requires one.

citations.label: NOAA: export requirements by country (G–M), South Korea

rules.agency: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), Office of Law Enforcement
rules.title: Wildlife declaration and licence: shellfish and non-living fishery products exported for human or animal consumption need no USFWS declaration or licence and may leave from any port, unless the species needs an ESA or CITES permit. Live fish exported for other purposes, such as glass eels (elvers) shipped to fish farms, need a Form 3-177 declaration filed before export, a USFWS import/export licence and, as a rule, a designated port.

citations.label: 50 CFR 14.21 (shellfish and fishery products: any port)

rules.agency: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Division of Management Authority
rules.title: CITES export permit: species listed in CITES Appendix II need a U.S. CITES export permit before they ship, whatever the purpose. For seafood this mostly means sharks (requiem sharks and hammerheads, as frozen fish, meat or fins), sturgeon and paddlefish, and queen conch. American eels are not CITES-listed, so live glass eels need no CITES permit.

groups.label: Live fish
groups.note: Mostly live eels and ornamental fish. Glass eels for fish farms need a USFWS declaration and licence; South Korea and China want a NOAA health certificate for live fish; sturgeon and paddlefish need a CITES permit.

groups.label: Fresh or chilled whole fish
groups.note: Fresh salmon and halibut go mostly to Canada, which needs a NOAA aquatic-animal-health certificate only for certain wild marine products. EU and China sales need a listed plant and a NOAA health certificate.

groups.label: Frozen whole fish
groups.note: Frozen salmon, roe, pollock, flatfish and cod for Asia and the EU: a NOAA health certificate and a listed plant for China and the EU, MFDS plant registration for Korea. Frozen sharks need a CITES permit for listed species.

groups.label: Fish fillets & other fish meat
groups.note: Pollock fillets for the EU need an FDA-listed plant, a NOAA EU health certificate and a Legal Harvest document; surimi for Korea needs MFDS plant registration.

groups.label: Dried, salted & smoked fish
groups.note: Smoked and salted fish follow the destination's certificate rules; fins of CITES-listed sharks need a CITES permit.

groups.label: Crustaceans: shrimp, lobster, crab
groups.note: Live lobster needs a NOAA health certificate (the live-product version) for China and most Asian buyers and a listed plant for China and the EU. Japan asks for a paralytic shellfish poison control plan for lobster with tomalley and a Legal Harvest certificate for cooked crab.

groups.label: Molluscs: scallops, squid, oysters, clams
groups.note: Geoduck and other live clams for China and Hong Kong, and frozen squid for China: a NOAA health certificate and listed plant for China. Live raw oysters for Japan need a NOAA health certificate and come only from approved states; Australia has required an FDA certificate for bivalves since February 16, 2026. Queen conch needs a CITES permit.

groups.label: Sea cucumbers, sea urchins & other aquatic invertebrates
groups.note: Sea cucumbers and sea urchins, mostly to Hong Kong, China and Japan: a NOAA health certificate where the buyer requires one, and a registered plant for China.

savings.title: Claim the free-trade-agreement rate abroad
savings.saves: The partner country's tariff on qualifying U.S. goods — often 0% instead of its normal rate.
savings.appliesTo: Goods that meet the agreement's rules of origin, shipped to one of the 20 U.S. free-trade-agreement partners: Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Oman, Panama, Peru and Singapore.
savings.document: A certification of origin from the exporter, producer or importer, which the buyer uses to claim the rate at import. For USMCA there is no set form, but it must contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A.
savings.caveat: Whoever certifies must be able to back it up: for USMCA, a U.S. exporter or producer keeps origin records for at least 5 years, gives CBP a copy on request and tells buyers promptly about errors. Check the product's rule of origin and the partner's rate in the FTA Tariff Tool first.

savings.title: Get U.S. duty back on imported inputs (drawback)
savings.saves: 99% of the U.S. import duties, taxes and fees paid on goods or materials that are exported, or used to make the goods you export.
savings.appliesTo: Imported goods exported unused, and imported materials used to make an exported product (or, under the substitution rules, goods of the same kind).
savings.document: An electronic drawback claim in ACE, filed within 5 years of the import date, with the import and export records that tie the two together.
savings.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refunded, and CBP takes no paper claims. The refund is on U.S. duties only; it does not lower the buyer's tariff.

savings.title: Use the EU's duty-free quotas for U.S. pollock, salmon, squid and hake
savings.saves: The EU's normal duty on U.S. seafood within the quota: 15% on frozen whole Alaska pollock, 13.7% on frozen pollock fillets, 14.2% on frozen pollock meat and 2% on frozen Pacific salmon.
savings.appliesTo: U.S.-origin frozen Alaska pollock, pollock fillets and pollock meat (340,000 t a year), frozen Pacific salmon and salmon fillets (20,000 t), frozen squid (5,000 t) and frozen hake fillets and dogfish (20,000 t), from July 1, 2026.
savings.document: The EU importer declares the quota preference with U.S. origin and proves non-preferential U.S. origin (document code U190), for example by showing the goods came directly from the U.S. or stayed under customs supervision in transit.
savings.caveat: Each quota is first come, first served and runs in 12-month periods from July 1; once it is used up the normal duty applies. The preferences end on December 31, 2029 unless renewed, and the Commission can suspend them. Lobster needs no quota: the EU charges 0% on live, frozen and processed lobster from every country under Regulation (EU) 2026/1461.

citations.label: Access2Markets: EU duties on U.S. goods from July 1, 2026

savings.title: Have your Chinese buyer use China's tariff exclusion process
savings.saves: China's 2018–19 counter-tariffs on U.S. seafood (25% plus 5%), which come on top of its normal rate and its extra 10% on all U.S. goods. Live lobster pays 17% instead of 47%.
savings.appliesTo: Crustaceans of heading 0306 (lobster, crab, shrimp), which are all on China's list of goods eligible for exclusion; other seafood only if the buyer gets the item added.
savings.document: The Chinese importer applies under China's market-based exclusion process for an approved purchase amount; the U.S. exporter supplies the product and origin details.
savings.caveat: Exclusions are valid until December 31, 2026, with no extension announced. They do not remove China's extra 10% on all U.S. goods.

citations.label: Tariff Commission Announcement No. 2 of 2020 (market-based exclusion process)
White House fact sheet on the U.S.–China deal (Nov 1, 2025)

disclaimer: This page summarizes U.S. export rules to help you find the right regulation; it is not legal advice. Rules change and depend on the exact product, buyer and destination — check the cited regulation and the agency before you ship.
